questions.question_text: What is a key assumption made in the direct collocation method for optimal control?
questions.answer: Um, so, I think a key assumption in the direct collocation method is that, uh, the system dynamics are, like, continuous over the time intervals. I mean, it kinda involves breaking down the control problem into discrete points, right? And then it assumes that the state and control inputs can be approximated really well by, um, polynomial functions or something like that. This way, you can, like, evaluate the system behavior at those points and then optimize it. But, um, I’m not totally sure about all the details – it gets pretty complex!

questions.question_text: What is an open-loop control in the context of deterministic problems?
questions.answer:
Um, so open-loop control, in the context of deterministic problems, is like, um, a method where you just decide on a sequence of actions or inputs without really adjusting them based on the feedback from the system. It's, um, kind of like setting a plan and sticking to it, right? 

In deterministic settings, you know that the outcomes will be predictable, so you don’t have to worry about, um, uncertainty or noise affecting your decisions. So, I think you just optimize your actions ahead of time, and that's your policy. It's really about finding the best path to take based on the model you have. But, um, I might not have all the details right.

questions.question_text: What is an open-loop control in the context of deterministic problems?
questions.answer:
Um, so, I think open-loop control in deterministic problems is, like, when you have a system and you can just apply a sequence of actions without really needing feedback from the system. It’s, um, kind of like a pre-planned strategy where you optimize your actions ahead of time. 

Since the system is deterministic, the outcomes are predictable, so you can just calculate the best actions to take. Um, I guess this is linked to optimization because you’re finding the best way to achieve your goal without adjusting as you go. But, I'm not entirely sure about all the details, like how exactly the optimization part works.
